dabble.etymology: Freq. of dab: cf. OD. dabbelen.

dabchick.etymology: For dabchick. See Dap, Dip, cf. Dipchick.

dace.etymology: Written also dare, dart, fr. F. dard dase, dart, of German origin. Dace is for an older darce, fr. an OF. nom. darz. See Dart a javelin.

dachshund.etymology: G., from dachs badger + hund dog.

dad.etymology: Prob. of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. daid, Gael. daidein, W. tad, OL. , , Skr. tata.

dado.etymology: It. dado die, cube, pedestal; of the same origin as E. die, n. See Die, n.

daedal.etymology: L. daedalus cunningly wrought, fr. Gr. ; cf. to work cunningly. The word also alludes to the mythical Dædalus (Gr. , lit., the cunning worker).

daffodil.etymology: OE. affodylle, prop., the asphodel, fr. LL. affodillus (cf. D. affodille or OF. asphodile, aphodille, F. asphodèle), L. asphodelus, fr. Gr. . The initial d in English is not satisfactorily explained. See Asphodel.

daft.etymology: OE. daft, deft, deft, stupid; prob. the same word as E. deft. See Deft.

dag.etymology: Cf. F. dague, LL. daga, D. dagge (fr. French); all prob. fr. Celtic; Cf. Gael. dag a pistol, Armor. dag dagger, W. dager, dagr, Ir. daigear. Cf. Dagger.

dagger.etymology: Cf. OE. daggen to pierce, F. daguer. See Dag a dagger.

dagon.etymology: Heb. Dagon, fr. dag a fish: cf. Gr. .

roots.meaning: A combining form signifying impressed form; stamp; print; type; typical form; representative; as in stereotype phototype, ferrotype, monotype.

dahlia.etymology: Named after Andrew Dahl a Swedish botanist.

daily.etymology: AS. dæglic; dæg day + -lic like. See Day.

dainty.etymology: OE. deinie, dainte, deintie, deyntee, OF. deintié delicacy, orig., dignity, honor, fr. L. dignitas, fr. dignus worthy. See Deign, and cf. Dignity.

dairy.etymology: OE. deierie, from deie, daie, maid; of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. deigja maid, dairymaid, Sw. deja, orig., a baking maid, fr. Icel. deig. Dough.

dais.etymology: OE. deis, des, table, dais, OF. deis table, F. dais a canopy, L. discus a quoit, a dish (from the shape), LL., table, fr. Gr. a quoit, a dish. See Dish.

daisy.etymology: OE. dayesye, AS. dæges day's eye, daisy. See Day, and Eye.

dale.etymology: AS. dæl; akin to LG., D., Sw., Dan., OS., & Goth. dal, Icel. dalr, OHG. tal, G. thal, and perth. to Gr. a rotunda, Skr. dhara depth. Cf. Dell.

dally.etymology: OE. , dailien; cf. Icel. pylja to talk, G. dallen, dalen, dahlen, to trifle, talk nonsense, OSw. tule a droll or funny man; or AS. dol foolish, E. dull.

dam.etymology: OE. dame mistress, lady; also, mother, dam. See Dame.

damage.etymology: OF. damage, domage, F. dommage, fr. assumed LL. damnaticum, from L. damnum damage. See Damn.

damascene.etymology: L. Damascenus of Damascus, fr. Damascus the city, Gr. . See Damask, and cf. Damaskeen, Damaskin, Damson.

damask.etymology: From the city Damascus, L. Damascus, Gr. , Heb. Dammesq, Ar. Daemeshq; cf. Heb. d'meseq damask; cf. It. damasco, Sp. damasco, F. damas. Cf. Damascene, DamassÉ.

dame.etymology: F. dame, LL. domna, fr. L. domina mistress, lady, fem. of dominus master, ruler, lord; akin to domare to tame, subdue. See Tame, and cf. Dam mother, Dan, Danger, Dangeon, Dungeon, Dominie, Don, n., Duenna.

damn.etymology: OE. damnen dap), OF. damner, dampner, F. damner, fr. L. damnare, damnatum, to condemn, fr. damnum damage, a fine, penalty. Cf. Condemn, Damage.

damnable.etymology: L. damnabilis, fr. damnare: cf. F. damnable. See Damn.

damnation.etymology: F. damnation, L. damnatio, fr. damnare. See Damn.

damnatory.etymology: L. damnatorius, fr. damnator a condemner.

damp.etymology: Akin to LG., D., & Dan. damp vapor, steam, fog, G. dampf, Icel. dampi, Sw. damb dust, and to MNG. dimpfen to smoke, imp. dampf.

damsel.etymology: OE. damosel, damesel, damisel, damsel, fr. OF. damoisele, damisele, gentlewoman, F. demoiselle young lady; cf. OF. damoisel young nobleman, F. damoiseau; fr. LL. domicella, dominicella, fem., domicellus, dominicellus, masc., dim. fr. L. domina, dominus. See Dame, and cf. Demoiselle, Doncella.

damson.etymology: OE. damasin the Damascus plum, fr. L. Damascenus. See Damascene.

dance.etymology: F. danser, fr. OHG. dans to draw; akin to dinsan to draw, Goth. apinsan, and prob. from the same root (meaning to stretch) as E. thin. See Thin.

dandelion.etymology: F. dent de lion lion's tooth, fr. L. dens tooth + leo lion. See Tooth, n., and Lion.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

dandle.etymology: Cf. G. dändeln to trifly, dandle, OD. & Prov. G. danten, G. tand trifly, prattle; Scot. dandill, dander, to go about idly, to trifly.

dandruff.etymology: Prob. from W. toncrust, peel, skin + AS. dr dirty, draffy, or W. drwg bad: cf. AS. tan a letter, an eruption. sq. root240.

dandy.etymology: Cf. F. dandin, ninny, silly fellow, dandiner to waddle, to play the fool; prob. allied to E. dandle. Senses 2&3 are of uncertain etymol.

danger.etymology: OE. danger, daunger, power, arrogance, refusal, difficulty, fr. OF. dagier, dongier (with same meaning), F. danger danger, fr. an assumed LL. dominiarium power, authority, from L. dominium power, property. See Dungeon, Domain, Dame.

dangerous.etymology: OE., haughty, difficult, dangerous, fr. OF. dangereus, F. dangereux. See Danger.

dangle.etymology: Akin to Dan. dangle, dial. Sw. dangla, Dan. dingle, Sw. dingla, Icel. dingla; perh. from E. ding.

dank.etymology: Cf. dial, Sw. dank a moist place in a field, Icel. dökk pit, pool; possibly akin to E. damp or to daggle dew.

daphne.etymology: L., a laurel tree, from Gr. .

dapper.etymology: OE. daper; prob. fr. D. dapper brave, valiant; akin to G. tapfer brave, OHG. taphar heavy, weighty, OSlav. dobrû good, Russ. dobrui. Cf. Deft.

dapple.etymology: Cf. Icel. depill a spot, a dot, a dog with spots over the eyes, dapi a pool, and E. dimple.

dardanian.etymology: From L. Dardania, poetic name of Troy.

dare.etymology: OE. I dar, dear, I dare, imp. dorste, durste, AS. ic dear I dare, imp. dorste. inf. durran; akin to OS. gidar, gidorsta, gidurran, OHG. tar, torsta, turran, Goth. gadar, gadaúrsta, Gr. tharsei^n, tharrei^n, to be bold, tharsy`s bold, Skr. Dhrsh to be bold. sq. root70.

dark.etymology: OE. dark, derk, deork, AS. dearc, deorc; cf. Gael. & Ir. dorch, dorcha, dark, black, dusky.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

darling.etymology: OE. derling, deorling, AS. deórling; deóre dear + -ling. See Dear, and -ling.

darlingtonia.etymology: NL. Named after Dr. William Darlington, a botanist of West Chester, Penn.

darn.etymology: OE. derne, prob. of Celtic origin; cf. W. darnio to piece, break in pieces, W. & Arm. to E. tear. Cf. Tear, v. t.

darnel.etymology: OE. darnel, dernel, of uncertain origin; cf. dial. F. darnelle, Sw. dår-repe; perh. named from a supposed intoxicating quality of the plant, and akin to Sw. dåra to infatuate, OD. door foolish, G. thor fool, and Ee. dizzy.

dart.etymology: OF. dart, of German origin; cf. OHG. tart javelin, dart, AS. dara, daro, Sw. dart dagger, Icel. darra dart.

darwinian.etymology: From the name of Charles Darwin, an English scientist.

dash.etymology: Of. Scand. origin; cf. Dan daske to beat, strike, Sw. & Icel. daska, Dan. & Sw. dask blow.

dastard.etymology: Prob. from Icel. dæstr exhausted. breathless, p. p. of dæsa to groan, lose one's breath; cf. dasask to become exhausted, and E. daze.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

dasyure.etymology: Gr. thick, shaggy + tail: cf. F. dasyure.

date.etymology: F. datte, L. dactylus, fr. Gr. , prob. not the same word as finger, but of Semitic origin.

dative.etymology: L. dativus appropriate to giving, fr. dare to give. See 2d Date.

datura.etymology: NL.; cf. Skr. dhatt, Per. & Ar. tat, Tat.

daub.etymology: OE. dauben to smear, OF. dauber to plaster, fr. L. dealbare to whitewash, plaster; de- + albare to whiten, fr. albus white, perh. also confused with W. dwb plaster, dwbio to plaster, Ir. & OGael. dob plaster. See Alb, and cf. Dealbate.

daughter.etymology: OE. doughter, doghter, dohter, AS. dohtor, dohter; akin to OS. dohtar, D. dochter, G. tochter, Icel. d, Sw. dotter, Dan. dotter, datter, Goth. daúhtar,, OSlav. d, Russ. doche, Lith. dukt, Gr. , Zendughdhar, Skr. duhit; possibly originally, the milker, cf. Skr. duh to milk. sq. root68, 245.

daunt.etymology: OF. danter, F. dompter to tame, subdue, fr. L. domitare, v. intens. of domare to tame. See Tame.

dauphin.etymology: F. dauphin, prop., a dolphin, from L. delphinus. See Dolphin. The name was given, for some reason unexplained, to Guigo, count of Vienne, in the 12th century, and was borne by succeeding counts of Vienne. In 1349, Dauphiny was bequeathed to Philippe de Valois, king of France, on condition that the heir of the crown should always hold the title of Dauphin de Viennois.

davenport.etymology: From the name of the original maker. Encyc. Dict.

davit.etymology: Cf. F. davier forceps, davit, cooper's instrument, G. david davit; all probably from the proper name David.

daw.etymology: OE. dawe; akin to OHG. taha, MHG. tahe, tahele, G. dohle. Cf. Caddow.

day.etymology: OE. day, dai,, dei, AS. dæg; akin to OS., D., Dan., & Sw. dag, G, tag, Icel. dagr, Goth. dags; cf. Skr. dah (for dhagh ) to burn. *69. Cf. Dawn.

daze.etymology: OE. dasen, prob. from Icel. dasask to become weary, a reflexive verb; cf. Sw. dasa to lie idle, and OD. daesen to be foolish, insane, daes, dwaes, D. dwaas, foolish, insane, AS. dw, dysig, stupid. Dizzy, Doze.

deacon.etymology: OE. diakne, deakne, deken, AS. diacon, deacon, L. diaconus, fr. Gr. dean.

dead.etymology: OE. ded, dead, deed, AS. deád; akin to OS. d, D. dood, G. todt, tot, Icel. dau, Sw. & Dan. död, Goth. daubs; prop. p. p. of an old verb meaning to die. See Die, and cf. Death.

deaden.etymology: From Dead; cf. AS. d to kill, put to death. See Dead, a.

deaf.etymology: OE. def, deaf, deef, AS. deáf; akin to D. doof, G. taub, Icel. daufr, Dan. döv, Sw. döf, Goth. daubs, and prob. to E. dumb (the original sense being, dull as applied to one of the senses), and perh. to Gr. toben to rage. Cf. Dumb.

deal.etymology: OE. del, deel, part, AS. d; akin to OS. d, D. & Dan. deel, G. theil, teil, Icel. deild, Sw. del, Goth. dails. Dole.

dealfish.etymology: From deal a long, narrow plank.

dean.etymology: OE. dene, deene, OF. deien, dien, F. doyen, eldest of a corporation, a dean, L. decanus the chief of ten, one set over ten persons, e. g., over soldiers or over monks, from decem ten. See Ten, and cf. Decemvir.

dear.etymology: OE. dere, deore, AS. deóre; akin to OS. diuri, D. duur, OHG. tiuri, G. theuer, teuer, Icel. d, Dan. & Sw. dyr. Cf. Darling, Dearth.

dearth.etymology: OE. derthe, fr. dere. See Dear.

death.etymology: OE. deth, dea, AS. deá; akin to OS. d, D. dood, G. tod, Icel. dau, Sw. & Dan. död, Goth. daupus; from a verb meaning to die. See Die, v. i., and cf. Dead.

debacle.etymology: F. débâcle, fr. débâcler to unbar, break loose; pref. dé- (prob. = L. dis) + bâcler to bolt, fr. L. baculum a stick.

debark.etymology: F. débarquer; pref. dé- (L. dis-) + barque. See Bark the vessel, and cf. Disbark.

debase.etymology: Pref. de- + base. See Base, a., and cf. Abase.

debate.etymology: OF. debatre, F. débattre; L. de + batuere to beat. See Batter, v. t., and cf. Abate.

debauch.etymology: F. débaucher, prob. originally, to entice away from the workshop; pref. dé- (L. dis- or de) + OF. bauche, bauge, hut, cf. F. bauge lair of a wild boar; prob. from G. or Icel., cf. Icel. balkr. See Balk, n.

debauchee.etymology: F. dé, n., properly p. p. of débaucher. See Debauch, v. t.

debenture.etymology: L. debentur they are due, fr. debere to owe; cf. F. debentur. So called because these receipts began with the words Debentur mihi.

debile.etymology: L. debilis: cf. F. débile. See Debility.

debilitate.etymology: L. debilitatus, p. p. of debilitare to debilitate, fr. debilis. See Debility.

debility.etymology: L. debilitas, fr. debilis weak, prob. fr. de- + habilis able: cf. F. débilité. See Able, a.

debit.etymology: L. debitum what is due, debt, from debere to owe: cf. F. débit. See Debt.

debonair.etymology: OE. debonere, OF. de bon aire, debonaire, of good descent or lineage, excellent, debonair, F. débonnaire debonair; de of (L. de) + bon good (L. bonus) + aire. See Air, and Bounty, and cf. Bonair.

debouch.etymology: F. déboucher; pref. dé- (L. dis- or de) + boucher to stop up, fr. bouche mouth, fr. L. bucca the cheek. Cf. Disembogue.

debris.etymology: F., fr. pref. dé- (L. dis) + briser to break, shatter; perh. of Celtic origin.

debt.etymology: OE. dette, F. dette, LL. debita, fr. L. debitus owed, p. p. of debere to owe, prop., to have on loan; de- + habere to have. See Habit, and cf. Debit, Due.

debut.etymology: F. début, prop., the first cast or throw at play, fr. but aim, mark. See Butt an end.

debutante.etymology: F., p. pr. of débuter to have the first throw, to make one's début. See Début.

decade.etymology: F. décade, L. decas, -adis, fr. Gr. Ten.

decadence.etymology: LL. decadentia; L. de- + cadere to fall: cf. F. décadence. See Decay.

decalogue.etymology: F. décalogue, L. decalogus, fr. Gr. Ten.

decameter.etymology: F. décamètre; Gr. mètre. See Meter.

decametre.etymology: F. décamètre; Gr. mètre. See Meter.

decamp.etymology: F. décamper; pref. dé- (L. dis) + camp camp. See Camp.

decant.etymology: F. décanter (cf. It. decantare), prop., to pour off from the edge of a vessel; pref. dé- (L. de) + OF. cant (It. canto) edge, border, end. See Cant an edge.

decapitate.etymology: LL. decapitatus, p. p. of decapitare; L. de- + caput head. See Chief.

deceive.etymology: OE. deceveir, F. décevoir, fr. L. decipere to catch, insnare, deceive; de- + capere to take, catch. See Capable, and cf. Deceit, Deception.

december.etymology: F. décembre, from L. December, fr. decem ten; this being the tenth month among the early Romans, who began the year in March. See Ten.

decency.etymology: L. decentia, fr. decens: cf. F. décence. See Decent.

decennary.etymology: L. decennium a period of ten years; decem ten + annus a year.

decent.etymology: L. decens, decentis, p. pr. of decere to be fitting or becoming; akin to decus glory, honor, ornament, Gr. d to grant, to give; and perh. akin to E. attire, tire: cf. F. décent. Cf. Decorate, Decorum, Deig.

deception.etymology: F. déception, L. deceptio, fr. decipere, deceptum. See Deceive.

decide.etymology: L. decidere; de- + caedere to cut, cut off; prob. akin to E. shed, v.: cf. F. décider. Cf. Decision.

decigram.etymology: F. décigramme; pref. déci- tenth (fr. L. decimus) + gramme.

decile.etymology: F. décil, fr. L. decem tendecile.

deciliter.etymology: F. décilitre; pref. déci- tenth (L. decimus) + litre. See Liter.

decilitre.etymology: F. décilitre; pref. déci- tenth (L. decimus) + litre. See Liter.

decimal.etymology: F. décimal (cf. LL. decimalis), fr. L. decimus tenth, fr. decem ten. See Ten, and cf. Dime.

decimate.etymology: L. decimatus, p. p. of decimare to decimate (in senses 1 & 2), fr. decimus tenth. See Decimal.

decimeter.etymology: F. décimètre; pref. déci- tenth (fr. L. decimus) + mètre. See Meter.

decimetre.etymology: F. décimètre; pref. déci- tenth (fr. L. decimus) + mètre. See Meter.

decision.etymology: L. decisio, fr. decidere, decisum: cf. F. décision. See Decide.

deck.etymology: D. dekken to cover; akin to E. thatch. See Thatch.

dimension.etymology: L. dimensio, fr. dimensus, p. p. of dimetiri to measure out; di- = dis- + metiri to measure: cf. F. dimension. See Measure.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

diminish.etymology: Pref. di- (= L. dis-) + minish: cf. L. diminuere, F. diminuer, OE. diminuen. See Dis-, and Minish.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

diminuendo.etymology: It., p. pr. of diminuere to diminish.

diminution.etymology: L. diminutio, or perh. rather deminutio: cf. F. diminution. See Diminish.

dimity.etymology: Prob. fr. Gr. diemet, of F. dimite, démitte. Cf. Samite.

dimple.etymology: Prob. a nasalized dim. of dip. See Dip, and cf. Dimble.

din.etymology: AS. dyne, dyn; akin to Icel. dynr, and to AS. dynian to resound, Icel. dynja to pour down like hail or rain; cf. Skr. dhuni roaring, a torrent, dhvan to sound. Cf. Dun to ask payment.

dinar.etymology: Ar. d, from Gr. denarius. See Denier.

dine.etymology: F. dîner, OF. disner, LL. disnare, contr. fr. an assumed disjunare; dis- + an assumed junare (OF. juner) to fast, for L. jejunare, fr. jejunus fasting. See Jejune, and cf. Dinner, D.

ding.etymology: OE. dingen, dengen; akin to AS. dencgan to knock, Icel. dengja to beat, hammer, Sw. dänga, G. dengeln.

dingle.etymology: Of uncertain origin: cf. AS. ding prison; or perh. akin to dimble.

dinner.etymology: F. dîner, fr. dîner to dine. See Dine.

dint.etymology: OE. dint, dent, dunt, a blow, AS. dynt; akin to Icel. dyntr a dint, dynta to dint, and perh. to L. fendere (in composition). Cf. 1st Dent, Defend.

diocese.etymology: OE. diocise, OF. diocise, F. diocése, L. dioecesis, fr. Gr. Economy.

dioscorea.etymology: NL. Named after Dioscorides the Greek physician.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

dip.etymology: OE. dippen, duppen, AS. dyppan; akin to Dan. dyppe, Sw. doppa, and to AS. d to baptize, OS. d, D. doopen, G. taufen, Sw. döpa, Goth. daupjan, Lith. dubus deep, hollow, OSlav. dupl hollow, and to E. dive. Cf. Deep, Dive.

diphtheria.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. membrane): cf. depsere to knead.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

diplomacy.etymology: F. diplomatie. This word, like supremacy, retains the accent of its original. See Diploma.

diplomatist.etymology: Cf. F. diplomatiste a student of diplomatics.

roots.meaning: A New Latin plural combining form or suffix from Gr. foot; as, hexapoda, myriapoda. See -pod.
A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

direct.etymology: L. directus, p. p. of dirigere to direct: cf. F. direct. See Dress, and cf. Dirge.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying full of, abounding with; as, boastful, harmful, woeful.

dirge.etymology: Contraction of Lat. dirige, direct thou (imperative of dirigere), the first word of a funeral hymn (Lat. transl. of Psalm v. 8) beginning, "Dirige, Domine, in conspectu tuo vitam meam." See Direct, a., and cf. Dirige.

dirt.etymology: OE. drit; kin to Icel. drit excrement, drita to dung, OD. drijten to dung, AS. gedritan.

disabuse.etymology: Pref. dis- + abuse; cf. F. désabuser.

disaccord.etymology: Cf. F. désaccorder to cause discord.

disafforest.etymology: Pref. dis- + afforest: cf. OF. desaforester.

disagree.etymology: Pref. dis- + agree: cf. F. désagréer to displease.

disagreement.etymology: Cf. F. désagrément disagreeable circumstance, disagreeableness.

disallow.etymology: Pref. dis- + allow: cf. OF. desalouer, desloer, to blame, dissuade.

disappoint.etymology: OF. desapointier, F. désappointer; pref. des- (L. dis-) + apointier, F. appointier, to appoint. See Appoint.

disapprobation.etymology: Pref. dis- + approbation: cf. F. désapprobation. Cf. Disapprove.

disapprove.etymology: Pref. dis- + approve: cf. F. déapprouver. Cf. Disapprobation.

disarm.etymology: OE. desarmen, F. désarmer; pref. dés- (L. dis-) + armer to arm. See Arm.

disarrange.etymology: Pref. dis- + arrange: cf. F. désarranger.

disarray.etymology: Pref. dis- + array, v.: cf. OF. desarroyer, desarreier.

disaster.etymology: F. désastre; pref. dés- (L. dis-) + astre star, fr. L. astrum; a word of astrological origin. See Aster, Astral, Star.

disavow.etymology: F. désavouer; pref. dés- (L. dis-) + avouer to avow. See Avow, and cf. Disavouch.

disband.etymology: Pref. dis- + band: cf. OF. desbander, F. débander, to unbind, unbend. See Band, and cf. Disbend, Disbind.

disburse.etymology: OF. desbourser, F. débourser; pref. des- (L. dis- ) + bourse purse. See Burse, and cf. Dispurse.

discalceate.etymology: L. discalceatus unshod; dis- + calceus shoe.

discern.etymology: F. discerner, L. discernere, discretum; dis- + cernere to separate, distinguish. See Certain, and cf. Discreet.

discerp.etymology: L. discerpere, discerptum; dis- + carpere to pluck.

discharge.etymology: OE. deschargen, dischargen, OF. deschargier, F. décharger; pref. des- (L. dis) + chargier, F. charger. See Charge.

disciple.etymology: OE. disciple, deciple, OF. disciple, fr. L. discipulus, fr. discere to learn (akin to docere to teach; see Docile) + prob. a root meaning to turn or drive, as in L. pellere to drive (see Pulse).

disciplinary.etymology: LL. disciplinarius flogging: cf. F. disciplinaire.

discipline.etymology: F. discipline, L. disciplina, from discipulus. See Disciple.

disclose.etymology: OE. desclosen, disclosen, fr. disclos, desclos, not shut in, open, OF. desclos, p. p. of desclore to open, F. déclore; pref. des- (L. dis-) + clore to shut, fr. L. claudere to shut. See Close, and cf. Disclusion.

disclosure.etymology: See Disclose, v. t., and cf. Closure.

discolor.etymology: OE. descolouren, OF. descolorer, F. décolorer, fr. L. dis- + cololare, coloratum, to color, color color. See Color.

discomfit.etymology: OF. desconfit, p. p. of desconfire, F. déconfire; fr. L. dis- + conficere to make ready, prepare, bring about. See Comfit, Fact.

discomfiture.etymology: OF. desconfiture, F. déconfiture. See Discomfort, v. t., and cf. Comfiture.

discomfort.etymology: OF. desconforter, F. déconforter, to discourage; pref. des- (L dis-) + conforter. See Comfort.

discompose.etymology: Pref. dis- + compose: cf. OF. decomposer, F. décomposer.

disconcert.etymology: Pref. dis- + concert: cf. OF. desconcerter, F. déconcerter.

disconsolate.etymology: LL. disconsolatus; L. dis- + consolatus, p. p. of consolari to console. See Console, v. t.

discord.etymology: OE. discord, descord, OF. discorde, descorde, F. discorde, from L. discordia, fr. discors, -cordis, discordant, disagreeable; dis- + cor, cordis, heart; cf. F. discord, n., and OF. descorder, discorder, F. discorder, to discord, L. discordare, from discors. See Heart, and cf. Discord, v. i.

discordant.etymology: OE. discordant, descordaunt, OF. descordant, discordant, F. discordant, p. pr. of discorder, OF. also, descorder. See Discord, n.

discount.etymology: OF. desconter, descompter, to deduct, F. décompter to discount; pref. des- (L. dis-) + conter, compter. See Count, v.

discountenance.etymology: Pref. dis- + countenance: cf. OF. descontenancer, F. décontenancer.

discourage.etymology: Pref. dis- + courage: cf. OF. descoragier, F. décourager: pref. des- (L. dis-) + corage, F. courage. See Courage.

discourse.etymology: L. discursus a running to and fro, discourse, fr. discurrere, discursum, to run to and fro, to discourse; dis- + currere to run: cf. F. discours. See Course.

discourteous.etymology: Pref. dis- + courteous: cf. OF. discortois.

discourtesy.etymology: Pref. dis- + courtesy: cf. OF. descourtoisie.

discover.etymology: OE. discoveren, discuren, descuren, OF. descovrir, descouvrir, F. découvrir; des- (L. dis-) + couvrir to cover. See Cover.

discreet.etymology: F. discret, L. discretus separated (whence the meaning reserved, prudent), p. p. of discernere. See Discern, and cf. Discrete.

discrepancy.etymology: L. disrepantia: cf. OF. discrepance. See Discrepant.

discrepant.etymology: L. discrepans, -antis, p. pr. of discrepare to sound differently or discordantly; dis- + crepare to rattle, creak: cf. OF. discrepant. See Crepitate.

discrete.etymology: L. discretus, p. p. of discernere. See Discreet.

discretion.etymology: F. discrétion, L. discretio separation, difference, discernment, fr. discernere, discretum. See Discreet, Discern.

discriminate.etymology: L. discriminatus, p. p. of discriminare to divide, separate, fr. discrimen division, distinction, decision, fr. discernere. See Discern, and cf. Criminate.

discrimination.etymology: L. discriminatio the contrasting of opposite thoughts.

discursive.etymology: Cf. F. discursif. See Discourse, and cf. Discoursive.

discuss.etymology: L. discussus, p. p. of discutere to strike asunder (hence came the sense to separate mentally, distinguish); dis- + quatere to shake, strike. See Quash.

discussion.etymology: L. discussio a shaking, examination, discussion: cf. F. discussion.

disdain.etymology: OE. desdain, disdein, OF. desdein, desdaing, F. dédain, fr. the verb. See Disdain, v. t.

disease.etymology: OE. disese, OF. desaise; des- (L. dis-) + aise ease. See Ease.

disembark.etymology: Pref. dis- + embark: cf. F. désembarquer.

disembarrass.etymology: Pref. dis- + embarrass: cf. F. désembarasser.

disenchant.etymology: Pref. dis- + enchant: cf. F. désenchanter.

disenchantment.etymology: Pref. dis- + enchantment: cf. F. désenchantement.

disencumber.etymology: Pref. dis- + encumber: cf. F. désencombrer.

disengage.etymology: Pref. dis- + engage: cf. F. désengager.

disengagement.etymology: Pref. dis- + engagement: cf. F. désengagement.

disfavor.etymology: Pref. dis- + favor: cf. OF. disfaveur, F. défaveur.

disfigure.etymology: OF. desfigurer, F. défigurer; pref. des- (L. dis-) + figurer to fashion, shape, fr. L. figurare, fr. figura figure. See Figure, and cf. Defiguration.

disgorge.etymology: F. dégorger, earlier desgorger; pref. dé-, des- (L. dis-) + gorge. See Gorge.

disgrace.etymology: F. disgrâce; pref. dis- (L. dis-) + grâce. See Grace.

disguise.etymology: OE. desguisen, disgisen, degisen, OF. desguisier, F. déguiser; pref. des- (L. dis-) + guise. See Guise.

disgust.etymology: OF. desgouster, F. dégoûter; pref. des- (L. dis-) + gouster to taste, F. goûter, fr. L. gustare, fr. gustus taste. See Gust to taste.

dish.etymology: AS. disc, L. discus dish, disc, quoit, fr. Gr. Dais, Desk, Disc, Discus.

dishevel.etymology: OF. descheveler, F. décheveler, LL. discapillare; dis- + L. capillus the hair of the head. See Capillary.

dishonest.etymology: Pref. dis- + honest: cf. F. déshonnête, OF. deshoneste.

dishonor.etymology: OE. deshonour, dishonour, OF. deshonor, deshonur, F. déshonneur; pref. des- (L. dis-) + honor, honur, F. honneur, fr. L. honor. See Honor.

disintegrate.etymology: L. dis- + integratus, p. p. of integrare to renew, repair, fr. integer entire, whole. See Integer.

disjoin.etymology: OF. desjoindre, F. disjoindre, déjoindre, fr. L. disjungere; dis- + jungere to join. See Join, and cf. Disjoint, Disjunct.

disjoint.etymology: OF. desjoint, p. p. of desjoindre. See Disjoin.

disjunct.etymology: L. disjunctus, p. p. of disjungere to disjoin. See Disjoin, and cf. Disjoint.

dislocate.etymology: LL. dislocatus, p. p. of dislocare; dis- + locare to place, fr. locus place. See Locus.

dislodge.etymology: OF. deslogier, F. déloger; pref. des- (L. dis-) + OF. logier, F. loger. See Lodge.

disloyal.etymology: Pref. dis- + loyal: cf. OF. desloial, desleal, F. déloyal. See Loyal.

disloyalty.etymology: Pref. dis- + loyalty: cf. OF. desloiauté, deslealté, F. déloyauté.

dismal.etymology: Formerly a noun; e. g., "I trow it was in the dismalle." Chaucer. Of uncertain origin; but perh. (as suggested by Skeat) from OF. disme, F. dîme, tithe, the phrase dismal day properly meaning, the day when tithes must be paid. See Dime.

dismantle.etymology: F. démanteler, OF. desmanteler; pref: des- (L. dis-) + manteler to cover with a cloak, defend, fr. mantel, F. manteau, cloak. See Mantle.

dismay.etymology: OE. desmaien, dismaien, OF. esmaier; pref. es- (L. ex) + OHG. magan to be strong or able; akin to E. may. In English the pref. es- was changed to dis- (L. dis-). See May, v. i.

dismember.etymology: OF. desmembrer, F. démembrer; pref. des- (L. dis) + OF. & F. membre limb. See Member.

dismiss.etymology: L. dis- + missus, p. p. of mittere to send: cf. dimittere, OF. desmetre, F. démettre. See Demise, and cf. Dimit.

dismount.etymology: Pref. dis- + mount: cf. OF. desmonter, F. démonter.

disobedient.etymology: Pref. dis- + obedient. See Disobey, Obedient.

disobey.etymology: F. désobéir; pref. dés- (L. dis-) + obéir. See Obey, and cf. Disobedient.

disoblige.etymology: Pref. dis- + oblige: cf. F. désobliger.

disorder.etymology: Pref. dis- + order: cf. F. désordre.

disorganization.etymology: Cf. F. désorganisation. See Disorganize, v. t.

disorganize.etymology: Pref. dis- + organize: cf. F. désorganiser.

disparage.etymology: OF. desparagier, F. déparager, to marry unequally; pref. des- (L. dis-) + F. parage extraction, lineage, from L. par equal, peer. See Peer.

disparate.etymology: L. disparatus, p. p. of disparare to part, separate; dis- + parare to make ready, prepare.

disparity.etymology: LL. disparitas, fr. L. dispar unlike, unequal; dis- + par equal: cf. F. disparité. See Par, Peer.

dispatch.etymology: OF. despeechier, F. dépêcher; prob. from pref. des- (L. dis-) + (assumed) LL. pedicare to place obstacles in the way, fr. L. pedica fetter, fr. pes, pedis, foot. See Foot, and cf. Impeach, Despatch.

dispel.etymology: L. dispellere; dis- + pellere to push, drive. See Pulse a beating.

dispense.etymology: F. dispenser, L. dispensare, intens. of dispendere. See Dispend.

disperse.etymology: L. dispersus, p. p. of dispergere to strew, scatter. See Sparse.

displace.etymology: Pref. dis- + place: cf. F. déplacer.

display.etymology: OE. displaien, desplaien, OF. despleier, desploier, F. déployer; pref. des- (L. dis-) + pleier, ploier, plier, F. ployer, plier, to fold, bend, L. plicare. See Ply, and cf. Deploy, Splay.

displease.etymology: OF. desplaisir, whence F. déplaisir displeasure; pref. des- (L. dis-) + plaisir to please. See Please, and cf. Displeasure.

displeasure.etymology: Pref. dis- + pleasure: cf. OF. desplaisir, F. déplaisir. Cf. Displease.

displume.etymology: Pref. dis- + plume: cf. OF. desplumer, F. déplumer.

disport.etymology: OF. desport, deport. See Disport, v. i., and cf. Sport.

dispose.etymology: F. disposer; pref. dis- + poser to place. See Pose.

disposition.etymology: F. disposition, dispositio, fr. disponere to dispose; dis- + ponere to place. See Position, and cf. Dispone.

dispossess.etymology: Pref. dis- + possess: cf. F. déposséder.

dispraise.etymology: OE. dispreisen, OF. desprisier, despreisier, F. dépriser; pref. des- (L. dis-) + prisier, F. priser, to prize, praise. See Praise, and cf. Disprize, Depreciate.

disproportion.etymology: Pref. dis- + proportion: cf. F. disproportion.

disprove.etymology: Pref. dis- + prove: cf. OF. desprover.

disputable.etymology: L. disputabilis: cf. F. disputable. See Dispute, v. i.

disputant.etymology: L. disputants, p. pr. of disputare: cf. F. disputant. See Dispute, v. i.

disputation.etymology: OE. desputeson, disputacion, OF. desputeison, F. disputation, fr. L. disputatio. See Dispute, v. i.

dispute.etymology: OE. desputen, disputen, OF. desputer, disputer, F. disputer, from L. disputare, disputatum; dis- + putare to clean; hence, fig., to clear up, set in order, reckon, think. See Putative, Pure.

disquisition.etymology: L. disquisitio, fr. disquirere to inquire diligently, investigate; dis- + quaerere to seek. See Quest.

disrupt.etymology: L. disruptus, diruptus, p. p. of disrumpere, to break or burst asunder; dis- + rumpere to break, burst. See Rupture.

dissect.etymology: L. dissectus, p. p. of dissecare; dis- + secare to cut. See Section.

dissemble.etymology: OF. dissembler to be dissimilar; pref. dis- (L. dis-) + F. sembler to seem, L. simulare to simulate; cf. L. dissimulare to dissemble. See Simulate, and cf. Dissimulate.

disseminate.etymology: L. disseminatus, p. p. of disseminare to disseminate; dis- + seminare to sow, semen seed. See Seminary.

dissension.etymology: L. dissensio: cf. F. dissension. See Dissent.

dissent.etymology: L. dissentire, dissentum; dis- + sentire to feel, think. See Sense.

dissentient.etymology: L. dissentiens, p. pr. of dissentire. See Dissent, v. i.

dissertate.etymology: L. dissertatus, p. p. of dissertare to discuss, intents, fr. disserere. See Dissert.

disservice.etymology: Pref. dis- + service: cf. F. desservice.

dissever.etymology: OE. dessevrer; pref. des- (L. dis-) + sevrer to sever, F. sevrer to wean, L. separate to separate. In this word the prefix is intensive. See Dis-, and Sever.

dissidence.etymology: L. dissidentia: cf. F. dissidence. See Dissident, a.

dissident.etymology: L. dissidens, -entis, p. pr. of dissidere to sit apart, to disagree; dis- + sedere to sit: cf. F. dissident. See Sit.

dissilient.etymology: L. dissiliens, -entis, p. pr. of dissilire to leap asunder: dis- + salire to leap.

dissimilar.etymology: Pref. dis- + similar: cf. F. dissimilaire.

dissimilitude.etymology: L. dissimilitudo, fr. dissimilis: cf. F. dissimilitude.

dissimulate.etymology: L. dissimulatus, p. p. of dissimulare. See Dissemble.

dissipate.etymology: L. dissipatus, p. p. of dissipare; dis- + an obsolete verb sipare, supare. to throw.

dissociable.etymology: L. dissociabilis, fr. issociare: cf. F. dissociable. See Dissociate.

dissociate.etymology: L. dissociatus, p. p. of dissociare to dissociate; dis- + sociare to unite, associate, socius companion. See Social.

dissoluble.etymology: L. dissolubilis: cf. F. dissoluble. See Dissolve, and cf. Dissolvable.

dissolute.etymology: L. dissolutus, p. p. of dissolvere: cf. F. dissolu. See Dissolve.

dissolution.etymology: OE. dissolucioun dissoluteness, F. dissolution, fr. L. dissolutio, fr. dissolvere. See Dissolve.

dissolve.etymology: L. dissolvere, dissolutum; dis- + solvere to loose, free. See Solve, and cf. Dissolute.

dissolvent.etymology: L. dissolvens, -entis, p. pr. of dissolvere.

dissonant.etymology: L. dissonans, -antis, p. pr. of dissonare to disagree in sound, be discordant; dis- + sonare to sound: cf. F. dissonant. See Sonant.

dissuade.etymology: L. dissuadere, dissuasum; dis- + suadere to advise, persuade: cf. F. dissuader. See Suasion.

dissuasion.etymology: L. dissuasio: cf. F. dissuasion. See Dissuade.

dissyllable.etymology: F. dissyllabe, L. disyllabus, adj., of two syllables, fr. Gr. Syllable.

distaff.etymology: OE. distaf, dysestafe, AS. distaef; cf. LG. diesse the bunch of flax on a distaff, and E. dizen. See Staff.

distant.etymology: F., fr. L. distans, -antis, p. pr. of distare to stand apart, be separate or distant; dis- + stare to stand. See Stand.

distemper.etymology: OF. destemprer, destremper, to distemper, F. détremper to soak, soften, slake (lime); pref. des- (L. dis-) + OF. temprer, tremper, F. tremper, L. temperare to mingle in due proportion. See Temper, and cf. Destemprer.

distend.etymology: L. distendere, distentum, distensum; dis- + tendere to stretch, stretch out: cf. F. distendre to distend, détendre to unbend. See Tend, and cf. Detent.

distich.etymology: L. distichon, Gr. stigan to ascend: cf. F. distique. See Stirrup.

distill.etymology: F. distiller, from L. destillare, destillatum; de + stillare to drop, stilla a drop, prob. fr. stiria frozen drop, icicle; prob. akin to stare, E. stand. Cf. Still, n. & v., Instill.

distinct.etymology: L. distinctus, p. p. of distinguere: cf. F. distinct. See Distinguish.

distinguish.etymology: F. distinguer, L. distinguere, distinctum; di- = dis- + stinguere to quench, extinguish; prob. orig., to prick, and so akin to G. stechen, E. stick, and perh. sting. Cf. Extinguish.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

distort.etymology: L. distortus, p. p. of distorquere to twist, distort; dis- + torquere to twist. See Torsion.

distract.etymology: L. distractus, p. p. of distrahere to draw asunder; dis- + trahere to draw. See Trace, and cf. Distraught.

distrain.etymology: OE. destreinen to force, OF. destreindre to press, oppress, force, fr. L. distringere, districtum, to draw asunder, hinder, molest, LL., to punish severely; di- = stringere to draw tight, press together. See Strain, and cf. Distress, District, Distraint.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

distraught.etymology: OE. distract, distrauht. See Distract, a.

distress.etymology: OE. destresse, distresse, OF. destresse, destrece, F. détresse, OF. destrecier to distress, (assumed) LL. districtiare, fr. L. districtus, p. p. of distringere. See Distrain, and cf. Stress.

distribute.etymology: L. distributus, p. p. of distribuere to divide, distribute; dis- + tribuere to assign, give, allot. See Tribute.

disturb.etymology: OE. desturben, destourben, OF. destorber, desturber, destourber, fr. L. disturbare, disturbatum; dis- + turbare to disturb, trouble, turba disorder, tumult, crowd. See Turbid.

disunion.etymology: Pref. dis- + union: cf. F. désunion.

ditch.etymology: OE. dich, orig. the same word as dik. See Dike.

dittany.etymology: OE. dytane, detane, dytan, OF. ditain, F. dictame, L. dictamnum, fr. Gr. Dicte in Crete. Cf. Dittander.

ditto.etymology: It., detto, ditto, fr. L. dictum. See Dictum.

ditty.etymology: OE. dite, OF. ditié, fr. L. dictatum, p. p. neut. of dictare to say often, dictate, compose. See Dictate, v. t.

diurnal.etymology: L. diurnalis, fr. dies day. See Deity, and cf. Journal.

divagation.etymology: L. divagari to wander about; di- = dis- + vagari to stroll about: cf. F. divagation. See Vagary.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

divalent.etymology: Pref. di- + L. valens, valentis, p. pr. See Valence.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

divan.etymology: Per. diwan a book of many leaves, an account book, a collection of books, a senate, council: cf. Ar. daiwan, F. divan.

divaricate.etymology: L. divaricatus, p. p. of divaricare to stretch apart; di- = dis- + varicare to straddle, fr. varicus straddling, fr. varus stretched outwards.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

dive.etymology: OE. diven, duven, AS. d to sink, v. t., fr. d, v. i.; akin to Icel. d, G. taufen, E. dip, deep, and perh. to dove, n. Cf. Dip.

diverge.etymology: L. di- = dis- + vergere to bend, incline. See Verge.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

divers.etymology: F. divers, L. diversus turned in different directions, different, p. p. of divertere. See Divert, and cf. Diverse.

diverse.etymology: The same word as divers. See Divers.

diversify.etymology: F. diversifier, LL. diversificare, fr. L. diversus diverse + ficare (in comp.), akin to facere to make. See Diverse.

diversity.etymology: F. diversité, L. diversitas, fr. diversus. See Diverse.

divert.etymology: F. divertir, fr. L. divertere, diversum, to go different ways, turn aside; di- = dis- + vertere to turn. See Verse, and cf. Divorce.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

divest.etymology: LL. divestire (di- = dis- + L. vestire to dress), equiv. to L. devestire. It is the same word as devest, but the latter is rarely used except as a technical term in law. See Devest, Vest.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

divide.etymology: L. dividere, divisum; di- = dis- + root signifying to part; cf. Skr. vyadh to pierce; perh. akin to L. vidua widow, and E. widow. Cf. Device, Devise.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

dividend.etymology: L. dividendum thing to be divided, neut. of the gerundive of dividere: cf. F. dividende.

divination.etymology: L. divinatio, fr. divinare, divinatum, to foresee, foretell, fr. divinus: cf. F. divination. See Divine.

divinity.etymology: F. divinité, L. divinitas. See Divine, a.

divisible.etymology: L. divisibilis, fr. dividere: cf. F. divisible. See Divide.

division.etymology: F. division, L. divisio, from dividere. See Divide.

divorce.etymology: F. divorce, L. divortium, fr. divortere, divertere, to turn different ways, to separate. See Divert.

divulge.etymology: F. divulguer, L. divulgare; di- = dis- + vulgare to spread among the people, from vulgus the common people. See Vulgar.

roots.meaning: A prefix, signifying twofold, double, twice; (Chem.)

dizen.etymology: Perh. orig., to dress in a foolish manner, and allied to dizzy: but cf. also OE. dysyn (Palsgrave) to put tow or flax on a distaff, i. e., to dress it. Cf. Distaff.

dizzy.etymology: OE. dusi, disi, desi, foolish, AS. dysig; akin to LG. düsig dizzy, OD. deuzig, duyzig, OHG. tusig foolish, OFries. dusia to be dizzy; LG. dusel dizziness, duselig, dusselig, D. duizelig, dizzy, Dan. dösig drowsy, slepy, döse to make dull, drowsy, dös dullness, drowsiness, and to AS. dw foolish, G. thor fool. Daze, Doze.

docent.etymology: L. docens, -entis, p. pr. of docere to teach.

docile.etymology: L. docilis,fr. docere to teach; cf. Gr. discere to learn, Gr. docile. Cf. Doctor, Didactic, Disciple.

docility.etymology: L. docilitas, fr. docilis: cf. F. docilité.

dock.etymology: AS. docce; of uncertain origin; cf. G. docken- blätter, Gael. dogha burdock, OF. doque; perh. akin to L. daucus, daucum, Gr. Burdock.

docket.etymology: Dock to cut off + dim. suffix -et.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix with a diminutive force; as in baronet, pocket, facet, floweret, latchet.

doctor.etymology: OF. doctur, L. doctor, teacher, fr. docere to teach. See Docile.

doctrinal.etymology: LL. doctrinalis, fr. L. doctrina: cf. F. doctrinal. See Doctrine.

doctrine.etymology: F. doctrine, L. doctrina, fr. doctor. See Doctor.

document.etymology: LL. documentum, fr. docere to teach: cf. F. document. See Docile.

dodder.etymology: Cf. Dan. dodder, Sw. dodra, G. dotter.

dodge.etymology: Of uncertain origin: cf. dodder, v., daddle, dade, or dog, v. t.

dodo.etymology: Said to be fr. Pg. doudo silly, foolish (cf. Booby); this is fr. Prov. E. dold, the same word as E. dolt.

doff.etymology: Do + off. See Do, v. t., 7.

dog.etymology: AS. docga; akin to D. dog mastiff, Dan. dogge, Sw. dogg.

dogbane.etymology: Said to be poisonous to dogs. Cf. Apocynaceous.

doge.etymology: It doge, dogio, for duce, duca, fr. L. dux, ducis, a leader, commander. See Duke.

dogma.etymology: L. dogma, Gr. pl. , fr. decet it is becoming. Cf. Decent.

dogmatize.etymology: L. dogmatizare to lay down an opinion, Gr. dogmatiser. See Dogma.

dogwood.etymology: So named from skewers (dags) being made of it. Dr. Prior. See Dag, and Dagger.

doily.etymology: So called from the name of the dealer.

dolce.etymology: It., fr. L. dulcis sweet, soft.

dole.etymology: OE. deol, doel, dol, OF. doel, fr. doloir to suffer, fr. L. dolere; perh. akin to dolare to hew.

doll.etymology: A contraction of Dorothy; or less prob. an abbreviation of idol; or cf. OD. dol a whipping top, D. dollen to rave, and E. dull.

dollar.etymology: D. daalder, LG. dahler, G. thaler, an abbreviation of Joachimsthaler, i. e., a piece of money first coined, about the year 1518, in the valley (G. thal) of St. Joachim, in Bohemia. See Dale.

dolmen.etymology: Armor. taol, tol, table + mean, maen, men, stone: cf. F. dolmen.

dolor.etymology: OE. dolor, dolur, dolour, F. douleur, L. dolor, fr. dolere. See 1st Dole.

dolorous.etymology: L. dolorosus, from dolor: cf. F. douloureux. See Dolor.

dolphin.etymology: F. dauphin dolphin, dauphin, earlier spelt also doffin; cf. OF. dalphinal of the dauphin; fr. L. delphinus, Gr. garbha; perh. akin to E. calf. Cf. Dauphin, Delphine.

dolt.etymology: OE. dulte, prop. p. p. of dullen to dull. See Dull.

domain.etymology: F. domaine, OF. demaine, L. dominium, property, right of ownership, fr. dominus master, owner. See Dame, and cf Demesne, Dungeon.

dome.etymology: F. dôme, It. duomo, fr. L. domus a house, domus Dei or Domini, house of the Lord, house of God; akin to Gr. timber. See Timber.

domestic.etymology: L. domesticus, fr. domus use: cf. F. domestique. See 1st Dome.

domesticate.etymology: LL. domesticatus, p. p. of domesticare to reside in, to tame. See Domestic, a.

domicile.etymology: L. domicilium; domus house + (prob.) root of celare to conceal: cf. F. domicile. See Dome, and Conceal.

dominant.etymology: L. dominans, -antis, p. pr. of dominari: cf. F. dominant. See Dominate.

dominate.etymology: L. dominatus, p. p. of dominari to dominate, fr. dominus master, lord. See Dame, and cf. Domineer.

domineer.etymology: F. dominer, L. dominari: cf. OD. domineren to feast luxuriously. See Dominate, v. t.

dominical.etymology: LL. dominicalis, for L. dominicus belonging to a master or lord (dominica dies the Lord's day), fr. dominus master or lord: cf. F. dominical. See Dame.

dominican.etymology: NL. Dominicanus, fr. Dominicus, Dominic, the founder: cf. F. Dominicain.

dominie.etymology: L. dominus master. See Don, Dame.

dominion.etymology: LL. dominio, equiv. to L. dominium. See Domain, Dungeon.

domino.etymology: F. domino, or It. dominò, or Sp. dominó, fr. L. dominus master. The domino was orig. a hood worn by the canons of a cathedral. See Don, Dame.

don.etymology: Sp. don; akin to Pg. dom, It. donno; fr. L. dominus master. See Dame, and cf. Domine, Dominie, Domino, Dan, Dom.

donate.etymology: L. donatus, p. p. of donare to donate, fr. donum gift, fr. dare to give. See 2d Date.

done.etymology: Prob. corrupted from OF. doné, F. donné, p. p. of OF. doner, F. donner, to give, issue, fr. L. donare to give. See Donate, and cf. Donee.

donee.etymology: OF. doné, F. donné, p. p. See the preceding word.

donkey.etymology: Prob. dun, in allusion to the color of the animal + a dim. termination.

donna.etymology: It. donna, L. domina. See Don, Dame.

donor.etymology: F. donneur, OF. daneor, fr. donner. See Donee, and cf. Donator.

doom.etymology: As. d; akin to OS. d, OHG. tuom, Dan. & Sw. dom, Icel. d, Goth. d, Gr. do, v. t. Do, v. t., and cf. Deem, -dom.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting: (a) Jurisdiction or property and jurisdiction, dominion, as in kingdom earldom. (b) State, condition, or quality of being, as in wisdom, freedom.

doomsday.etymology: AS. d. See Doom, and Day.

door.etymology: OE. dore, dure, AS. duru; akin to OS. dura, dor, D. deur, OHG. turi, door, tor gate, G. thür, thor, Icel. dyrr, Dan. dör, Sw. dörr, Goth. daur, Lith. durys, Russ. dvere, Olr. dorus, L. fores, Gr. dur, dvara. . Cf. Foreign.

dope.etymology: D. doop a dipping, fr. doopen to dip. Cf. Dip.

dorado.etymology: Sp. dorado gilt, fr. dorar to gild, fr. L. deaurare. See 1st Dory, and cf. Fl Dorado.

dormant.etymology: F., p. pr. of dormir to sleep, from L. dormire; cf. Gr. dra, OSlav. dr.

dormer.etymology: Literally, the window of a sleeping apartment. F. dormir to sleep. See Dormant, a. & n.

dormitory.etymology: L. dormitorium, fr. dormitorius of or for sleeping, fr. dormire to sleep. See Dormant.

dormouse.etymology: Perh. fr. F. dormir to sleep (Prov. E. dorm to doze) + E. mouse; or perh. changed fr. F. dormeuse, fem., a sleeper, though not found in the sense of a dormouse.

dorsal.etymology: F. dorsal, LL. dorsalis, fr. L. dorsualis, fr. dorsum back; cf. Gr. Dorse, Dorsel, Dosel.

dory.etymology: Named from 1st color, fr. F. dorée gilded, fr. dorer to gild, L. deaurare. See Deaurate, and cf. Aureole.

dose.etymology: F. dose, Gr. dare to give. See Date point of time.

dosser.etymology: LL. dosserum, or F.dossier bundle of papers, part of a basket resting on the back, fr. L. dorsum back. See Dorsal, and cf. Dosel.

dossier.etymology: F., back of a thing, bulging bundle of papers, fr. dos back.

dot.etymology: F., fr. L. dos, dotis, dowry. See Dower, and cf. Dote dowry.

double.etymology: OE. doble, duble, double, OF. doble, duble, double, F. double, fr. L. duplus, fr. the root of duo two, and perh. that of plenus full; akin to Gr. Two, and Full, and cf. Diploma, Duple.

doublet.etymology: In sense 3, OF. doublet; in sense 4, F. doublet, dim. of double double. See Double, a.

doubloon.etymology: F. doublon, Sp. doblon. See Double, a., and cf. Dupion.

doubt.etymology: OE. duten, douten, OF. duter, doter, douter, F. douter, fr. L. dubitare; akin to dubius doubtful. See Dubious.

douche.etymology: F., fr. It. doccia, fr. docciare to flow, pour, fr. an assumed LL. ductiare, fr. L. ducere, ductum, to lead, conduct (water). See Duct.

dough.etymology: OE. dagh, dogh, dow, AS. dah; akin to D. deeg, G. teig, Icel. deig, Sw. deg, Dan. deig, Goth. daigs; also, to Goth. deigan to knead, L. fingere to form, shape, Skr. dih to smear; cf. Gr. Feign, Figure, Dairy, Duff.

douse.etymology: Cf. Dowse, and OD. donsen to strike with the fist on the back, Sw. dunsa to fall down violently and noisily; perh. akin to E. din.

dove.etymology: OE. dove, duve, douve, AS. d; akin to OS. d, D. duif, OHG. t, G. taube, Icel. d, Sw. dufva, Dan. due, Goth. d; perh. from the root of E. dive.

dowager.etymology: OF. douagiere, fr. douage dower. See Dower.

dowdy.etymology: Scot. dawdie slovenly, daw, da sluggard, drab, Prov. E. dowd flat, dead.

dowel.etymology: Cf. G. döbel peg, F. douelle state of a cask, surface of an arch, douille socket, little pipe, cartridge.

dower.etymology: F. douaire, LL. dotarium, from L. dotare to endow, portion, fr. dos dower; akin to Gr. dare to give. See 1st Date, and cf. Dot dowry, Dotation.

down.etymology: Akin to LG. dune, dun, Icel. d, Sw. dun, Dan. duun, G. daune, cf. D. dons; perh. akin to E. dust.

downward.etymology: AS. ad. See Down, adv., and - ward.

downwards.etymology: AS. ad. See Down, adv., and - ward.

dowry.etymology: Contr. from dowery; cf. LL. dotarium. See Dower.

doxology.etymology: LL. doxologia, Gr. doxologie. See Dogma, and Legend.

doze.etymology: Prob. akin to daze, dizzy: cf. Icel. d to doze, Dan. döse to make dull, heavy, or drowsy, dös dullness, drowsiness, dösig drowsy, AS. dw dull, stupid, foolish. Dizzy.

dozen.etymology: OE. doseine, dosein, OF. doseine, F. douzaine, fr. douze twelve, fr. L. duodecim; duo two + decem ten. See Two, Ten, and cf. Duodecimal.

drab.etymology: AS. drabbe dregs, lees; akin to D. drab, drabbe, dregs, G. treber; for sense 1, cf. also Gael. drabag a slattern, drabach slovenly. Cf. Draff.

dragoman.etymology: From F. dragoman, or Sp. dragoman, or It. dragomanno; all fr. LGr. tarjuman, from the same source as E. targum. Cf. Drogman, Truchman.

dragon.etymology: F. dragon, L. draco, fr. Gr. dar to see), and so called from its terrible eyes. Cf. Drake a dragon, Dragoon.

dragoon.etymology: F. dragon dragon, dragoon, fr. L. draco dragon, also, a cohort's standard (with a dragon on it). The name was given from the sense standard. See Dragon.

drain.etymology: AS. drehnigean to drain, strain; perh. akin to E. draw.

drake.etymology: Akin to LG. drake, OHG. antrache, anetrecho, G. enterich, Icel. andriki, Dan. andrik, OSw. andrak, andrage, masc., and fr. AS. ened, fem., duck; akin to D. eend, G. ente, Icel. önd, Dan. and, Sw. and, Lith. antis, L. anas, Gr. ati a water fowl. rich. Cf. Gulaund.

dram.etymology: OF. drame, F. drachme, L. drachma, drachm, drachma, fr. Gr. Drachm, Drachma.

drape.etymology: F. draper, fr. drap cloth. See 3d Drab.

draught.etymology: The same as draft, the spelling with gh indicating an older pronunciation. See Draft, n., Draw.

dravidian.etymology: From Skr. Dravi, the name of the southern portion of the peninsula of India.

draw.etymology: OE. dra, drahen, draien, drawen, AS. dragan; akin to Icel. & Sw. draga, Dan. drage to draw, carry, and prob. to OS. dragan to bear, carry, D. dragen, G. tragen, Goth. dragan; cf. Skr. dhraj to move along, glide; and perh. akin to Skr. dhar to hold, bear. Drag, Dray a cart, 1st Dredge.

drawl.etymology: Prob. fr. draw: cf. D. dralen to linger, tarry, Icel. dralla to loiter. See Draw, and cf. Draggle.

dray.etymology: AS. dræge a dragnet, fr. dragan. . See Draw, and cf. 2d Drag, 1st Dredge.

dread.etymology: AS. dr, in comp.; akin to OS. dradan, OHG. tratan, both only in comp.

dream.etymology: Cf. AS. dr, dr, to rejoice. See Dream, n.

dreary.etymology: OE. dreori, dreri, AS. dreórig, sad; akin to G. traurig, and prob. to AS. dreósan to fall, Goth. driusan. Cf. Dross, Drear, Drizzle, Drowse.

dredge.etymology: F. drège, dreige, fish net, from a word akin to E. draw; cf. D. dreg, dregge, small anchor, dregnet dragnet. Draw.

dreg.etymology: Prob. from Icel. dregg; akin to Sw. drägg, cf. Icel. & Sw. draga to draw. Cf. Draw.

dreissena.etymology: NL. Named after Dreyssen, a Belgian physician.

drench.etymology: AS. drencan to give to drink, to drench, the causal of drincan to drink; akin to D. drenken, Sw. dränka, G. tränken. See Drink.

dress.etymology: OF. drecier to make straight, raise, set up, prepare, arrange, F. dresser. (assumed) LL. directiare, fr. L. dirigere, directum, to direct; dis- + regere to rule. See Right, and cf. Address, Adroit, Direct, Dirge.

dribble.etymology: Freq. of drib, which is a variant of drip.

drift.etymology: From drive; akin to LG. & D. drift a driving, Icel. drift snowdrift, Dan. drift, impulse, drove, herd, pasture, common, G. trift pasturage, drove. See Drive.

drill.etymology: D. drillen to bore, drill (soldiers); probably akin to AS. pyrlian, pyrelian, to pierce. See Thrill.

drilling.etymology: G. drillich, fr. L. trilix having three threads, fr. the of tres three + licium a thread of the warm. See Three, and cf. Twill.

drink.etymology: AS. drincan; akin to OS. drinkan, D. drinken, G. trinken, Icel. drekka, Sw. dricka, Dan. drikke, Goth. drigkan. Cf. Drench, Drunken, Drown.

drip.etymology: Akin to LG. drippen, Dan. dryppe, from a noun. See Drop.

drive.etymology: AS. drifan; akin to OS. driban, D. drijven, OHG. triban, G. treiben, Icel. drifa, Goth. dreiban. Cf. Drift, Drove.

drivel.etymology: Cf. OE. dravelen, drabelen, drevelen, drivelen, to slaver, and E. drabble. Cf. Drool.

drizzle.etymology: Prop. freq. of AS. dreósan to fall. See Dreary.

droll.etymology: F. drôle; cf. G. & D. drollig, LG. drullig, D. drol a thick and short person, a droll, Sw. troll a magical appearance, demon, trolla to use magic arts, enchant, Dan. trold elf, imp, Icel. tröll giant, magician, evil spirit, monster. If this is the origin, cf. Trull.

dromedary.etymology: F. dromadaire, LL. dromedarius, fr. L. dromas (sc. camelus), fr. Gr. dram to run.

drone.etymology: OE. drane a dronebee, AS. dran; akin to OS. dran, OHG. treno, G. drohne, Dan. drone, cf. Gr. Drone, v. i.

droop.etymology: Icel. dr; akin to E. drop. See Drop.

drop.etymology: OE. drope, AS. dropa; akin to OS. dropo, D. drop, OHG. tropo, G. tropfen, Icel. dropi, Sw. droppe; and Fr. AS. dreópan to drip, drop; akin to OS. driopan, D. druipen, OHG. triofan, G. triefen, Icel. drj. Cf. Drip, Droop.

dropsy.etymology: OE. dropsie, dropesie, OF. idropisie, F. hydropisie, L. hydropisis, fr. Gr. Water, and cf. Hydropsy.

drosky.etymology: Russ. drojki, dim. of drogi a kind of carriage, prop. pl. of droga shaft or pole of a carriage.

dross.etymology: AS. dros, fr. dreósan to fall. See Dreary.

drought.etymology: OE. droght, drougth, dru, AS. druga, from drugian to dry. See Dry, and cf. Drouth, which shows the original final sound.

drove.etymology: AS. draf, fr. drifan to drive. See Drive.

drown.etymology: OE. drunen, drounen, earlier drunknen, druncnien, AS. druncnian to be drowned, sink, become drunk, fr. druncen drunken. See Drunken, Drink.

drowse.etymology: AS. dr, dr, to sink, become slow or inactive; cf. OD. droosen to be sleepy, fall asleep, LG. dr, druusken, to slumber, fall down with a noise; prob, akin to AS. dreósan to fall. See Dreary.

drub.etymology: Cf. Prov. E. drab to beat, Icel. & Sw. drabba to hit, beat, Dan. dræbe to slay, and perh. OE. drepen to strike, kill, AS. drepan to strike, G. & D. freffen to hit, touch, Icel. drepa to strike, kill.

drudge.etymology: OE. druggen; prob not akin to E. drag, v. t., but fr. Celtic; cf. Ir. drugaire a slave or drudge.

drugget.etymology: F. droguet, prop. dim. of drogue trash, stuff, perh, the same word as drogue drug, but cf. also W. drwg evil, bad, Ir. & Gael. droch, Arm. droug, drouk. See 3d Drug.

druggist.etymology: F. droguiste, fr. drogue. See 3d Drug.

druid.etymology: L. Druides; of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. & Gael. draoi, druidh, magician, Druid, W. derwydd Druid.

drum.etymology: Cf. D. trom, trommel, LG. trumme, G. trommel, Dan. tromme, Sw. trumma, OHG. trumba a trumpet, Icel. pruma a clap of thunder, and as a verb, to thunder, Dan. drum a booming sound, drumme to boom; prob. partly at least of imitative origin; perh. akin to E. trum, or trumpet.

drumlin.etymology: Gael. druim the ridge of a hill.

drunk.etymology: OE. dronke, drunke, dronken, drunken, AS. druncen. Orig. the same as drunken, p. p. of drink. See Drink.

roots.meaning: The termination of many English words; as, coward, reynard, drunkard, mostly from the French, in which language this ending is of German origin, being orig. the same word as English hard. It usually has the sense of one who has to a high or excessive degree the quality expressed by the root; as, braggart, sluggard.

drunken.etymology: AS. druncen, prop., that has drunk, p. p. of drincan, taken as active. See Drink, v. i., and cf. Drunk.

druse.etymology: Cf. G. druse bonny, crystallized piece of ore, Bohem. druza. Cf. Dross.

dry.etymology: OE. dru, druye, drie, AS. dryge; akin to LG. dröge, D. droog, OHG. trucchan, G. trocken, Icel. draugr a dry log. Cf. Drought, Drouth, 3d Drug.

dryad.etymology: L. dryas, pl. dryades, Gr. Tree.

dual.etymology: L. dualis, fr. duo two. See Two.

dub.etymology: AS. dubban to strike, beat ("dubbade his sunu . . . to ridere." AS. Chron. an 1086); akin to Icel. dubba; cf. OF. adouber (prob. fr. Icel.) a chevalier, Icel. dubba til riddara.

dubiety.etymology: L. dubietas, fr. dubius. See Dubious.

dubious.etymology: L. dubius, dubiosus, fr. duo two. See Two, and cf. Doubt.

ducat.etymology: F. ducat, It. ducato, LL. ducatus, fr. dux leader or commander. See Duke.

duchy.etymology: F. duché, OF. duchée, (assumed) LL. ducitas, fr. L. dux. See Duke.

duck.etymology: Cf. Dan. dukke, Sw. docka, OHG. doccha, G. docke. Cf. Doxy.

duct.etymology: L. ductus a leading, conducting, conduit, fr. ducere, ductum, to lead. See Duke, and cf. Douche.

ductile.etymology: L. ductilis, fr. ducere to lead: cf. F. ductile. See Duct.

duds.etymology: Scot. dud rag, pl. duds clothing of inferior quality.

due.etymology: OF. deu, F. dû, p. p. of devoir to owe, fr. L. debere. See Debt, Habit, and cf. Duty.

duel.etymology: It. duello, fr. L. duellum, orig., a contest between two, which passed into the common form bellum war, fr. duo two: cf. F. duel. See Bellicose, Two, and cf. Duello.

duenna.etymology: Sp. dueña, doña, fr. L. domina. See Dame.

duffel.etymology: D. duffel, from Duffel, a town not far from Antwerp.

duke.etymology: F. duc, fr. L. dux, ducis, leader, commander, fr. ducere to lead; akin to AS. teón to draw; cf. AS. heretoga (here army) an army leader, general, G. herzog duke. See Tue, and cf. Doge, Duchess, Ducat, Duct, Adduce, Deduct.

dulcet.etymology: OF. doucet, dim. of dous sweet, F. doux, L. dulcis; akin to Gr. Doucet.

dulcify.etymology: L. dulcis sweet + -fy: cf. F. dulcifier.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

dulcimer.etymology: It. dolcemele,r Sp. dulcemele, fr. L. dulcis sweet + melos song, melody, Gr. doulcemele. See Dulcet, and Melody.

dulcinea.etymology: Sp., from Dulcinea del Toboso the mistress of the affections of Don Quixote.

dulcorate.etymology: L. dulcoratus, p. p. of dulcorare, fr. dulcor sweetness, fr. dulcis sweet.

dull.etymology: AS. dol foolish; akin to gedwelan to err, D. dol mad, dwalen to wander, err, G. toll mad, Goth. dwals foolish, stupid, cf. Gr. dhvr to cause to fall. Cf. Dolt, Dwale, Dwell, Fraud.

roots.meaning: The termination of many English words; as, coward, reynard, drunkard, mostly from the French, in which language this ending is of German origin, being orig. the same word as English hard. It usually has the sense of one who has to a high or excessive degree the quality expressed by the root; as, braggart, sluggard.

dulse.etymology: Cf. Gael. duileasg; duille leaf + uisge water. Cf. Whisky.

dumb.etymology: AS. dumb; akin to D. dom stupid, dumb, Sw. dumb, Goth. dumbs; cf. Gr. Deaf, and cf. Dummy.

dumpling.etymology: Dimin. of dump an illshapen piece; cf. D. dompelen to plunge, dip, duck, Scot. to dump in to plunge into, and E. dump, v. t.

dunce.etymology: From Joannes Duns Scotus, a schoolman called the Subtle Doctor, who died in 1308. Originally in the phrase "a Duns man". See Note below.

dunderhead.etymology: Prov. Eng. also dunderpoll, from dunder, same as thunder.

dune.etymology: The same word as down: cf. D. duin. See Down a bank of sand.

dung.etymology: AS. dung; akin to G. dung, dünger, OHG. tunga, Sw. dynga; cf. Icel. dyngja heap, Dan. dynge, MHG. tunc underground dwelling place, orig., covered with dung. Cf. Dingy.

dungeon.etymology: OE. donjoun highest tower of a castle, tower, prison, F. donjon tower or platform in the midst of a castle, turret, or closet on the top of a house, a keep of a castle, LL. domnio, the same word as LL. dominus lord. See Dame, Don, and cf. Dominion, Domain, Demesne, Danger, Donjon.

dunlin.etymology: Prob. of Celtic origin; cf. Gael. dun hill (E. dune), and linne pool, pond, lake, E. lin.

duo.etymology: It. duo, fr. L. duo two. See Duet.

duodenum.etymology: NL., fr. duodeni twelve each: cf. F. duodenum. So called because its length is about twelve fingers' breadth.

dupe.etymology: F., prob. from Prov. F. dupe, dube; of unknown origin; equiv. to F. huppe hoopoe, a foolish bird, easily caught. Cf. Armor. houpérik hoopoe, a man easily deceived. Cf. also Gull, Booby.

duplex.etymology: L., fr. duo two + plicare to fold. See Two, and Complex.

duplicate.etymology: L. duplicatus, p. p. of duplicare to double, fr. duplex double, twofold. See Duplex.

duplicity.etymology: F. duplicité, L. duplicitas, fr. duplex double. See Duplex.

durable.etymology: L. durabilis, fr. durare to last: cf. F. durable. See Dure.

duramen.etymology: L., hardness, a hardened, i. e., ligneous, vine branch, fr. durare to harden. See Dure.

durance.etymology: OF. durance duration, fr. L. durans, -antis, p. pr. durare to endure, last. See Dure, and cf. Durant.

durant.etymology: F. durant, p. pr. of durer to last. Cf. Durance.

durante.etymology: L., abl. case of the p. pr. of durare to last.

durbar.etymology: Hind. darbar, fr. Per dar house, court, hall of audience; dar door, gate + bar court, assembly.

duress.etymology: OF. duresse, du, hardship, severity, L. duritia, durities, fr. durus hard. See Dure.

dust.etymology: AS. dust; cf. LG. dust, D. duist meal dust, OD. doest, donst, and G. dunst vapor, OHG. tunist, dunist, a blowing, wind, Icel. dust dust, Dan. dyst mill dust; perh. akin to L. fumus smoke, E. fume. .

dutch.etymology: D. duitsch German; or G. deutsch, orig., popular, national, OD. dietsc, MHG. diutsch, tiutsch, OHG. diutisk, fr. diot, diota, a people, a nation; akin to AS. peód, OS. thiod, thioda, Goth. piuda; cf. Lith. tauta land, OIr. tuath people, Oscan touto. The English have applied the name especially to the Germanic people living nearest them, the Hollanders. Cf. Derrick, Teutonic.

dwarf.etymology: OE. dwergh, dwerf, dwarf, AS. dweorg, dweorh; akin to D. dwerg, MHG. twerc, G. zwerg, Icel. dvergr, Sw. & Dan. dverg; of unknown origin.

dwell.etymology: OE. dwellen, dwelien, to err, linger, AS. dwellan to deceive, hinder, delay, dwelian to err; akin to Icel. dvelja to delay, tarry, Sw. dväljas to dwell, Dan. dvæle to linger, and to E. dull. See Dull, and cf. Dwale.

dwindle.etymology: From OE. dwinen to languish, waste away, AS. dwinan; akin to LG. dwinen, D. dwijnen to vanish, Icel. dvina to cease, dwindle, Sw. tvina; of uncertain origin. The suffix -le, preceded by d excrescent after n, is added to the root with a diminutive force.

dyad.etymology: L. dyas, dyadis, the number two. Gr. dyade. See two, and cf. Duad.

dynamic.etymology: Gr. durus hard, E. dure: cf. F. dynamique.

dynamical.etymology: Gr. durus hard, E. dure: cf. F. dynamique.

dynast.etymology: L. dynastes, Gr. dynaste. See Dynamic.

dysentery.etymology: L. dysenteria, Gr. in: cf. F. dysenterie. See Dys, and In.

roots.meaning: An inseparable prefix, fr. the Greek ill, bad, hard, difficult, and the like; cf. the prefixes, Skr. dus-, Goth. tuz-, OHG. zur-, G. zer-, AS. to-, Icel. tor-, Ir. do-.

dyspepsia.etymology: L. dyspepsia, Gr. cook: cf. F. dyspepsie. See Dys-, and 3d Cook.
